sections.title: Malware Attack Indicators
sections.content:
MALWARE CLASSIFICATION BY VECTOR
Malware = software that does something bad from the system owner's perspective. Some classifications focus on the vector — the method by which malware executes and spreads:
Type | Description
Virus / Worm | Among the earliest malware types; spreads without user authorization by concealing itself in another process's executable code (the infected process)
Trojan | Malware concealed within an installer package for apparently legitimate software; seeks no consent and is designed to operate secretly
PUP/PUA (Potentially Unwanted Program/Application) | Installed alongside a chosen package or bundled with a new PC; not automatically malicious — may lack active consent or use confusing license terms. Also called grayware or bloatware
Other classifications are based on payload — the action performed beyond replication/persistence — e.g., spyware, rootkit, RAT, ransomware.
COMPUTER VIRUSES
A virus replicates and spreads by infecting executable applications or program code. Types by what they infect:
Virus Type | Behavior
Non-resident / file infector | Lives inside a host executable; infects other process images on storage, then returns control to the host program
Memory resident | Creates its own process in memory when the host file runs; persists even if the host process is terminated
Boot | Written to the disk boot sector/partition table; executes as memory-resident when the OS starts or media is attached
Script / macro | Uses local scripting engines (PowerShell, WMI, JavaScript, VBA-enabled Office docs, JavaScript-enabled PDFs)
• Multipartite — a virus using multiple vectors
• Polymorphic — a virus that dynamically changes/obfuscates its own code to evade detection
• Infected files spread via disk, network, email/social media attachments, or website downloads
WORMS AND FILELESS MALWARE
A worm is memory-resident malware that runs and replicates over the network without user intervention (unlike a virus, which needs the user to take some action). Example: Code Red exploited an IIS buffer overflow vulnerability and scanned random IP ranges to spread. Worms primarily consume bandwidth and can crash systems/apps (a DoS effect), and may carry any type of malicious payload.
Fileless malware (a descriptive term, not a strict classification) — illustrated by the Conficker worm's potency:
• Doesn't write its code to disk; runs via memory-resident techniques within its own process, a host process/DLL, or a scripting host (though registry changes for persistence may still occur, and initial execution may depend on a downloaded script/attachment/Trojan)
• Uses lightweight shellcode for a backdoor — easy to recompile in obfuscated form and download further payloads
• Uses "living off the land" techniques — legitimate tools like PowerShell and WMI to scan, reconfigure, and exfiltrate without needing compiled executables
Related terms: APT (advanced persistent threat), AVT (advanced volatile threat), LOC (low-observable characteristics) attack — the exact label matters less than recognizing that TTPs to evade detection continually evolve.
SPYWARE AND KEYLOGGERS
Type | Behavior
Tracking cookie | A plaintext file (not malware) that records web activity/IP/metadata via ad/analytics widgets
Supercookie / beacon | Harder-to-disable tracking — a supercookie stores data outside normal cookie declarations; a beacon is an invisible tracking pixel the browser must request
Adware | A PUP/bloatware class that reconfigures the browser (tracking cookies, default search provider, startup pages, bookmarks) via a program or extension
Spyware | Adware-like tracking plus local app monitoring, screenshots, mic/webcam activation, and DNS redirection to pharming sites
Keylogger | Spyware that actively steals confidential info by recording keystrokes (passwords, card data)
Keyloggers aren't only software — hardware devices can sit between keyboard and port (some with Wi-Fi exfiltration), plus wireless sniffers and overlay ATM pin pads.
BACKDOORS AND REMOTE ACCESS TROJANS
A backdoor is any access method that circumvents normal authentication and grants remote administrative control. A remote access Trojan (RAT) mimics legitimate remote-control software while operating covertly, allowing file upload, software install, or "living off the land" follow-on compromise. (RAT can also mean "remote administration tool.") A host under malicious control is a zombie.
• Bot — an automated script/tool performing malicious activity on a compromised host
• Botnet — a group of bots under one controller (herder), used for DDoS, spam campaigns, or cryptomining
• Command and control (C2/C&C) — the network connection a backdoor/bot uses to reach attacker infrastructure; usually the best way to detect the presence of a RAT/backdoor/bot. Historically IRC; modern methods hide commands in HTTPS or DNS traffic
• Backdoors can also arise from leftover developer/testing access or misconfiguration — not just malware
ROOTKITS
Malware inheriting only the logged-on user's privileges can be limited to that user's profile. To affect system-wide files, it needs local administrator privileges (via UAC confirmation or entered admin credentials). Critical Windows processes run at an even higher SYSTEM privilege level.
• Rootkit — malware that has escalated to run with SYSTEM (Windows) or root (UNIX/Linux, where "root" has unrestricted filesystem access) privileges — the term derives from UNIX/Linux
• May masquerade its process name to resemble a genuine executable (e.g., rund1132.exe vs. rundll32.exe); persistence typically requires a registry entry or service creation, which can usually be detected
• A rootkit can potentially compromise shell tools and programming interfaces (Explorer, taskmgr, tasklist on Windows; ps, top on Linux; netstat) so they no longer reveal its presence, and may clean system logs
• Some rootkits reside in firmware (device, adapter card, drive, or peripheral firmware) — these survive OS reinstall/reformat (e.g., the DarkMatter/QuarkMatter UEFI rootkits targeting Apple firmware)
• Ring architecture: Ring 0 = most privileged (kernel, direct hardware access); Ring 3 = user-mode processes; Rings 1–2 = drivers/I/O
RANSOMWARE, CRYPTO-MALWARE, AND LOGIC BOMBS
Ransomware extorts payment by making a victim's computer/data unavailable — payment via wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or premium-rate phone lines to avoid tracing.
• Scareware — displays alarming (often fake OS-style) alert messages to scare the user, without necessarily being true ransomware
• Crypto-ransomware — encrypts files on fixed/removable/network drives; the user cannot recover files without the attacker-held private key (e.g., CryptoLocker, which destroys the key after a countdown). Extremely difficult to mitigate without backups
• Cryptojacking — malware hijacks host resources to mine cryptocurrency (crypto-mining); often performed across botnets
• Logic bomb — triggers on a system/user event rather than automatically; a time bomb triggers on a preset date/time. Also called a mine. Not always malware code — e.g., a disgruntled admin's scripted trap set to run if their account is disabled; antivirus is unlikely to catch this kind of script
TTPS AND INDICATORS OF COMPROMISE
Signature-based antivirus detection is still important for commodity malware but is no longer wholly effective — modern detection increasingly relies on studying threat actor behaviors, described as TTPs:
Term | Level | Example
Tactic | High-level behavior | Reconnaissance, persistence, privilege escalation
Technique | Intermediate — how a tactic is carried out | Active network scanning, vulnerability scanning, email harvesting
Procedure | Detailed — how a technique is specifically performed | A particular actor's distinctive use of a specific tool
• Indicator of Compromise (IoC) — a residual sign that an asset/network has been successfully attacked or is continuing to be attacked; evidence of a TTP (e.g., a compromised process version, C2 connections, disabled backup features, ransom notices)
• Indicator of Attack (IoA) — evidence of an intrusion attempt in progress (as distinct from a completed/successful attack)
• The MITRE ATT&CK database (attack.mitre.org) is a well-known TTP/IoC reference; modern tools integrate threat feeds of published TTPs/indicators for automated behavioral scanning beyond simple signature matching
• IoCs can be objectively definite (a malware signature) or only identifiable via correlation of many anomalous data points — often requiring AI-backed analysis in modern threat platforms
MALICIOUS ACTIVITY INDICATORS
• Sandbox execution — analyze suspect code/hosts in an isolated environment that records file system/registry/network changes; a sheep dip is an isolated host used to test new software/removable media before production use
• Resource consumption — a performance monitor can reveal excessive/continuous CPU, memory leaks, disk I/O, disk space, or bandwidth use. Suggestive, not definitive (many non-malicious causes exist), but classically indicates botnet DDoS participation, cryptojacking, or crypto-ransomware
• File system — metadata (created/accessed/modified times) and suspicious temp files help build an incident timeline; blocked content indicators (denied ACL access, DLP blocks) reveal attempts to reach protected data
• Resource inaccessibility — a network/host/file/database becomes unavailable, typically indicating a DoS attack, resource exhaustion, ransomware, or malware disabling scanning/monitoring tools
• Account compromise indicators:
• Account lockout — too many failed attempts, or a threat actor changed the password
• Concurrent session usage — the account is signed in from two places at once
• Impossible travel — sign-in locations too far apart to have been reached physically in the elapsed time
• Logging indicators:
• Missing logs — deleted logs are easy to detect; a sophisticated actor instead removes select entries (watch for unusual timestamp gaps) or spoofs entries entirely
• Out-of-cycle logging — manipulating system time or log timestamps to hide activity

sections.title: Physical and Network Attack Indicators
sections.content:
PHYSICAL ATTACKS
A physical attack targets cabling, hardware, or site/facility environment.
• Brute force — smashing a device (physical DoS) or forcing a lock/cabinet (theft/tampering indicator). Theft often can't be prevented, so knowing something was stolen matters for breach reporting/permission revocation. Tamper-evident systems show visible, hard-to-disguise signs of forced entry
• Environmental — destroying power lines, cutting network cables, or disrupting cooling systems (a DoS attempt); building/environmental management systems are also a known vector for gaining network access
• RFID cloning/skimming — RFID (Radio Frequency ID) powers a passive tag when a reader is in range, often used for contactless building access:
• Cloning — physically duplicating a lost/stolen card that has no cryptographic protection; report loss immediately to revoke and reissue
• Skimming — using a counterfeit reader (potentially concealed on a person) to capture card/badge details and program a duplicate
• These attacks generally only work against "dumb" cards transmitting static tokens rather than performing cryptoprocessing; if card use is logged, compromise may show as impossible travel or concurrent use
• NFC (derived from RFID) works only at very close range and allows two-way communication between peers
NETWORK ATTACKS AND THE CYBERATTACK LIFECYCLE
A network attack disrupts or gains access via a network vector. Analysis is informed by where an attack type sits in the lifecycle (stages are iterative — a foothold enables repeating recon/harvesting internally):
Stage | Description
Reconnaissance | Host discovery (which IPs are live), service discovery (open ports), fingerprinting (app/OS versions); rapid scanning generates distinctive traffic, but is hard to distinguish from benign scanning
Credential harvesting | A recon subtype — learning passwords/cryptographic secrets for authenticated access
Denial of Service (DoS) | Causes hosts/services to become unavailable; may be an end in itself or a facilitator for other attacks
Weaponization, delivery, breach | Gaining unauthenticated access via malicious code directed at a vulnerable service, or tricking a user into running a malicious attachment
C2, beaconing, persistence | Remote operation of a compromised host over time; incoming commands/outgoing beaconing disguised as regular traffic (e.g., HTTPS). Detected via anomalous connection endpoints (e.g., countries with weak IP/privacy law enforcement) or host indicators like unauthorized startup items
Lateral movement, pivoting, privilege escalation | Moving host-to-host or segment-to-segment and gaining wider/higher permissions; detection usually depends on ML-backed tools since it's hard to distinguish from normal behavior
Data exfiltration | Copying an information asset to attacker infrastructure; large anomalous transfers may indicate it, but stealthy exfiltration can use small incremental transfers
DISTRIBUTED DENIAL OF SERVICE (DDOS) ATTACKS
A DoS attack reduces availability of a resource — malware-based DoS may destroy a file system or exhaust CPU/memory/storage/bandwidth. Network-layer DoS is typically distributed (DDoS) — launched from multiple compromised hosts (a botnet) simultaneously via a C2 network of handlers.
• Some DDoS variants simply consume bandwidth with overwhelming ordinary-looking requests; others exhaust CPU/memory via bombardment
• SYN flood — withholds the client's final ACK in the TCP three-way handshake, filling the target's limited pending-connection queue so it can't respond to legitimate traffic
Reflected and Amplified variants:
• Distributed Reflected DoS (DRDoS) — the attacker spoofs the victim's IP and opens connections with multiple third-party servers, which then direct their SYN/ACK responses at the victim, consuming its bandwidth (an example of an asymmetric threat — fewer resources than the victim, but still effective)
• Amplification attack — a reflected attack exploiting protocols that let the attacker manipulate a small request into a large forced response — commonly DNS, NTP, and CLDAP, plus attacks abusing the memcached database caching system
DDoS Indicators — traffic spikes with no legitimate explanation; usually mitigated via high-availability services (load balancing, clustering) rather than stopped at the source, since spoofed/botted source addresses make source-blocking difficult (though a stateful firewall can sometimes auto-detect and block).
ON-PATH ATTACKS
An on-path attack (formerly "man-in-the-middle," also adversary-in-the-middle/AitM) places the threat actor between two hosts to transparently capture, monitor, relay, or covertly modify communication — the hosts often can't detect the interception.
• ARP poisoning — a packet crafter (e.g., Ettercap) broadcasts unsolicited/gratuitous ARP replies; because ARP has no security mechanism, receiving devices trust the spoofed MAC:IP mapping and update their cache
• The usual target is the subnet's default gateway — if successful, all traffic destined for remote networks passes through the attacker
• Indicator: a pattern of gratuitous ARP traffic visible in a packet capture (e.g., Wireshark), including retransmission patterns between the victim and attacker MAC addresses
DOMAIN NAME SYSTEM ATTACKS
Public-facing DNS attacks include typosquatting, DRDoS abuse, direct DoS against DNS services, and hijacking a public server to insert spoofed records. On a private network, this is generally DNS poisoning:
Technique | Description
DNS-based on-path | Combines ARP poisoning with spoofed DNS replies; a rogue DHCP server can also configure clients with a malicious resolver address
DNS client cache poisoning | Planting false name:IP mappings in the local HOSTS file (/etc/hosts on Linux, %SystemRoot%\System32\Drivers\etc\hosts on Windows) — checked before DNS queries; requires admin access, so suspect entries indicate the machine is already compromised
DNS server cache poisoning | Corrupts records held by the DNS server itself, via DoS against the authoritative server plus spoofed replies, or by tricking the victim server into accepting false domain:IP mappings bundled with a legitimate-looking recursive query response
DNS Attack Indicators — the types of queries a host makes, hosts communicating with suspicious IP ranges/domains, and statistical anomalies like spikes or consistently high DNS lookup failures (which can also just mean malware, misconfiguration, or obsolete apps). DNS is also a popular channel for C2 and covert data exfiltration.
WIRELESS ATTACKS
• Rogue access point — installed without authorization (malicious or accidental, e.g., a tethered smartphone); creates a backdoor into the network if connected to a local segment
• Evil twin — a rogue AP masquerading as a legitimate one, using SSID typosquatting/stripping and potentially a spoofed BSSID (the AP radio's MAC address); may use DoS to overpower the legitimate AP, then harvest credentials or run on-path/DNS-redirection attacks
• Wireless DoS — RF interference/jamming (often unintentional, but can be deliberate with a stronger rogue signal); a disassociation attack exploits unencrypted management frames to spoof a disconnect notification targeting one station or broadcast to all stations — sometimes paired with a replay attack to recover the network key
• Wireless replay / key recovery — capturing handshake hashes for offline brute-force/dictionary cracking; the KRACK attack replays the WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake and works against both personal and enterprise auth modes — patching is the key mitigation
PASSWORD ATTACKS
A password attack exploits weaknesses in password selection/management to recover plaintext from a hash.
Attack Type | Description
Online | Interacts directly with the auth service (login form, VPN gateway); shows up as repeated failed logins followed by success, or logins at unusual times/locations. Mitigated by rate/attempt limiting — but this itself risks enabling DoS via account lockout
Offline | Attacker has obtained a password hash database (SAM, NTDS.DIT, /etc/shadow) or sniffed a challenge/response hash; doesn't interact with the live auth system. Indicator: file system audit logs showing access to these files, or attack tools present on the host
Brute force | Attempts every combination in the output space; effective mainly against short passwords, though GPU clusters extend reach to longer ones
Dictionary | Tests a dictionary of likely plaintexts against a captured hash — effective against noncomplex passwords
Hybrid | Combines dictionary + brute force (masks for numeric prefixes/suffixes) — targets naive passwords like james1
Password spraying | A horizontal online attack — tries one or more common passwords (e.g., password, 123456) against many usernames
CREDENTIAL REPLAY ATTACKS
Mostly target Windows Active Directory networks. Once signed into a domain, LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) caches secrets in memory/the SAM registry database to enable single sign-on:
• Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) and session key
• Service tickets for accessed applications
• NT hash of currently signed-in local/domain accounts (still used as the credential storage format even though NTLM itself is largely deprecated)
If multiple users (including privileged ones) are signed in on the same host, an attacker who compromises it may access all their cached secrets. LSASS purges hashes within minutes of sign-out; Credential Guard (available on some Windows editions) virtualizes protection of these secrets even from SYSTEM-level processes.
Attack | Description
Pass the Hash (PtH) | Uses a captured NT hash to start a session on another host still running a service (file sharing, RDP) that allows NTLM authentication
Golden ticket | Forges a Kerberos TGT — grants effectively unrestricted domain access
Silver ticket | Forges a Kerberos service ticket
(Golden/silver ticket attacks are both Pass the Ticket (PtT) attacks.) Mitigations: full patching, secure configuration baselines, disabling legacy NTLM where possible; detection can correlate security log event sequences (prone to false positives) or rely on AV/HIDS catching the credential-dumping/ticket-forgery malware itself.
CRYPTOGRAPHIC ATTACKS
• Downgrade attack — forces a server/client onto a lower-spec protocol with weaker ciphers/key lengths (e.g., forcing legacy SSL instead of TLS, easing forgery of a trusted CA's signature). Kerberoasting is a downgrade-style attack against Active Directory: it tries to force a service ticket to be returned with weak RC4 encryption (easy to brute force) instead of strong AES. Evidence typically appears in server logs or IDS alerts
• Collision attack — exploits a weak hashing function/implementation that allows two different plaintexts to produce the same digest, letting an attacker forge a signature: (1) create a malicious and a benign document with matching hashes, get the benign one signed, then (2) move that signature onto the malicious document
• Birthday attack — exploits hash collisions via brute force, informed by the birthday paradox (a group of just 23 people has a 50% chance two share a birthday — far fewer than the ~180 people intuition suggests). This means a mechanism generating enough plaintext variations can find a collision in a 128-bit hash space with roughly 2^64 attempts rather than the full 2^128

sections.title: Application Attack Indicators
sections.content:
APPLICATION ATTACKS — OVERVIEW
An application attack targets a design flaw (application vulnerability) that circumvents the app's security or crashes it. Two broad scenarios:
• Compromising the OS/third-party apps on a host (Trojans, malicious attachments, browser flaws) to gain a network foothold
• Compromising a website/web app to steal data or pivot further into the network
General indicators: increased application crashes/errors (logged in system or app-specific logs) and anomalous CPU/memory/storage/network use — both have non-malicious causes too, so correlate with other factors to pin down the specific attack type.
PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
A successful exploit lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution (or remote code execution, when the code originates from another machine) — typically to install a backdoor or disable the system.
Type | Description
Vertical privilege escalation | A user/app gains access to functionality/data above its authorized level (e.g., local admin process exploited to run as SYSTEM)
Horizontal privilege escalation | A user gains access to another user's functionality/data at the same privilege tier (e.g., a local admin process on a workstation ends up executing as a domain account on an application server)
Without real-time code/process analysis, privilege escalation attempts recorded in audit logs are often the simplest available indicator of an application attack; incident response and endpoint protection agents may also alert on this directly.
BUFFER OVERFLOW
A buffer is a reserved memory area expected to hold data of a certain size/format. An attacker deliberately overfills the buffer to overwrite adjacent memory. A stack overflow is a common variant — overwriting the subroutine's return address lets the attacker redirect execution to run arbitrary code.
• Mitigations: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), DEP (Data Execution Prevention)
• Indicator: frequent process crashes and anomalies from failed overflow attempts
REPLAY ATTACKS (SESSION HIJACKING)
HTTP is nominally stateless; cookies (name + value + optional security/expiry attributes) preserve state across requests — either nonpersistent (memory only, gone at browser close) or persistent (cached until deleted/expired). A session token uniquely identifies an authenticated user across requests.
• A replay attack captures or guesses a session token and resubmits it to illegitimately reestablish the session
• Vectors: sniffing via on-path attack or unsecured Wi-Fi, malware on the host, or cross-site scripting (XSS) — running malicious code in a browser in the context of a trusted site
• Session prediction — targets weaknesses in token-generation algorithms to anticipate future valid tokens; proper session management requires unpredictable tokens, no client info leakage, limited session lifespan, and periodic reauthentication
FORGERY ATTACKS
A forgery attack hijacks an authenticated session to perform an action without the user's consent (contrast with replay, which reestablishes the session itself).
Attack | Description
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) | Exploits cookie-based authentication — the attacker convinces the victim's browser to start a session with the target site, then passes a spoofed HTTP request (e.g., password/email change) that the target site accepts as genuine because a valid session cookie is present. Also called a confused deputy attack
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) | Causes a server application to process an arbitrary request targeting another internal or remote service, exploiting weak input validation and lack of authentication between internal servers/services. Common against cloud infrastructure with multi-tier architectures. Unlike CSRF (client's privilege level), an SSRF request runs at the server's privilege level
INJECTION ATTACKS
Client-side attacks (replay, CSRF, most XSS) run code in the browser; a server-side attack causes the server itself to process/run a script or query outside the intended application design — most commonly via an injection attack exploiting an unsecure request/query handling path.
Injection Type | Mechanism
XML External Entity (XXE) | Submits unencrypted/unvalidated XML defining an entity that points to a local resource (e.g., <!ENTITY bar SYSTEM "file:///etc/config">) — a successful attack returns the file's contents
LDAP injection | Exploits unsanitized input in (name=value) filter pairs joined by &/` | — e.g., entering bob)(&))` as a username can cause the password check to be logically dropped, bypassing authentication
Directory traversal | Requests a file outside the web root using ../ sequences; a canonicalization attack (e.g., percent-encoding as %2e%2e%2f) can disguise the traversal to bypass simple input filters
Command injection | Attempts to make the server execute OS shell commands and return the output, circumventing the restriction that server processes run with only a "guest"-level account
(SQL injection and persistent XSS are also injection attacks, covered under application/web security fundamentals.)
URL ANALYSIS
A URL can encode actions/data for the server beyond just a location — a common malicious vector.
• HTTP request = method + resource path + version + headers + body. Key methods: GET (retrieve), POST (submit for processing), PUT (create/replace)
• Data is submitted via POST/PUT body, or encoded directly in the URL after ? as name=value pairs joined by &
• Server responses include a version, status code, headers, and body (e.g., 200 "OK", 404 "Not Found")
• Percent encoding legitimately encodes reserved characters (: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =) or Unicode data that can't appear raw in a URL — but can be misused to obfuscate malicious input (encoding characters that don't need it) or to smuggle unsafe/control characters
WEB SERVER LOGS
Web servers typically log HTTP traffic that errors or matches a predefined rule set, preserving evidence of replay/forgery/injection attempts.
Status Code Range | Meaning | Example
4xx | Client-based error | Repeated 403 Forbidden — server rejecting unauthorized access attempts
5xx | Server-based error | 502 Bad Gateway — comms between servers blocked, or upstream server down
Some web servers also log HTTP header info for requests/responses (including cookie data), giving a detailed picture of each transaction for investigation. Access logs can also reveal automated scanning activity (e.g., a tool like Nikto generating multiple 404s while enumerating directories/files to map the attack surface).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Consider implementing behavior-based endpoint protection suites that can perform more effective detection of fileless malware
• Consider setting up a sandbox with analysis tools to investigate suspicious process behavior
• Consider using threat data feeds to assist with identification of documented and published indicators
• Implement inspection audits and site logging to identify brute force, environmental, and RFID cloning physical attacks
• Prepare playbooks and threat intelligence to assist with attack analysis
• Recognize resource consumption, file system anomalies, resource inaccessibility, and missing/out-of-cycle logging as indicators of system compromise
• Recognize lockout, concurrent session, and impossible travel as indicators of account compromise
• Know the characteristics of bloatware, virus, worm, Trojan, spyware, keylogger, ransomware, and logic bomb malware types
• Watch network appliance resource consumption for indicators of DDoS, including reflected and amplified types
• Use network monitoring and log data to identify on-path, DNS, wireless, credential replay, cryptographic downgrade, password spraying, and brute force password attacks
• Use host monitoring and logging to identify injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, and directory traversal application attacks

concept_cards.hook: Software detecting/removing viruses and other malware (worms, Trojans, rootkits, adware, spyware, password crackers, network mappers, DoS tools, etc.).
Network attack redirecting an IP address to the MAC address of an unintended host; enables DoS, spoofing, on-path attacks.
Indicator of malicious activity: audit logs show unauthorized attempts to read/copy data.
Indicator of malicious activity: account with multiple simultaneous sessions.

practice_questions.q: Many accounts each get one or two login attempts with the password 'Spring2026!'. What attack is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts.

practice_questions.q: An attacker uses usernames and passwords leaked from another site to log in to your company's portal. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Credential stuffing reuses leaked credentials across services.

practice_questions.q: A user logs in from New York and, ten minutes later, from Singapore. Which indicator is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Logins too far apart in too short a time suggest stolen credentials.

practice_questions.q: Malware that runs only in memory using built-in tools like PowerShell, leaving no file on disk, is called:
practice_questions.explanation: Fileless malware lives in memory and abuses legitimate tools.

practice_questions.q: Code planted by an insider deletes payroll data on a specific date if the insider is removed from the system. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: A logic bomb triggers when a condition is met.

practice_questions.q: Malware spreads across the network on its own by exploiting a vulnerable service, without any user action. What is it?
An attacker intercepts traffic between a user and a website and changes the data in transit. What attack is this?
practice_questions.explanation: An on-path attacker sits between two parties and can read or alter traffic.

practice_questions.q: An attacker forces a connection to use an older, weaker version of TLS. What attack is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Downgrade attacks push systems to weaker protocols.

practice_questions.q: A URL like /download?file=../../etc/passwd shows which attack?
practice_questions.explanation: The ../ sequences try to climb out of the web folder.

practice_questions.q: An attacker captures a valid authentication message and sends it again later to log in. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Replay attacks reuse captured valid data.
